Carlton room divider

Ettore Sottsass’s laminate bookcase from the first Memphis collection: a totem of tilted shelves in a dozen flat colors.

Context

The Art Institute describes the Carlton as a bookshelf and cabinet from the 1981 Memphis launch, made of wood and colored plastic laminate, 194.3 × 189.8 × 40 cm. AIC record.

The same record says the tiered form recalls “the head and arms of an ancient idol or totem” and links it to Sottsass’s laminate Superboxes of the 1960s for Poltronova. AIC record.

The Met holds another example, accession 1997.460.1a–d, dated 1981, wood and plastic laminate. Met record.

Observed

  • Shelves slant outward at about 45 degrees on each side, so the silhouette is a symmetrical fan of diagonals rather than a grid.
  • Each shelf and support has its own flat color: green, pale yellow, pink, light blue, red, dark blue, orange, black, gray, and brown.
  • A small red two-drawer cabinet sits at the center, under a pink triangle and a yellow tray topped by an empty square frame.
  • Small black triangles fill the joints where diagonal shelves meet horizontal ones.
  • The plinth is covered in a white laminate with dense black squiggle marks.

Why it belongs

The Carlton shows the Memphis method in one object: a useful bookcase is broken into parts, and each part gets a different color, so the object reads as a figure or a toy before it reads as storage.

The patterned base against the flat-colored shelves is the style’s pairing of printed surface and solid color.

Borrow

Give each structural part its own flat color and let diagonals carry the composition.

Put a busy black-and-white pattern on one base element as a foil for the solid colors above it.

Also from the first collection: Casablanca sideboard.
